text: to extract the resources. The result? For over four decades, every Alaskan resident has received an annual check. It is not welfare. It is a return on investment. The residents are the owners of the land and its resources; the oil companies pay to extract the oil and monetize it. They removed the government from the middle through distributed ownership. But Alaska is just one iteration. Look at Norway. There, the same resource—North Sea oil—built the Government Pension Fund Global. It is now the largest sovereign wealth fund in the world, owning nearly 1.5 percent of all listed companies on Earth. While the fund doesn’t pay out cash directly like Alaska, it effectively acts as a national savings account that makes every Norwegian a millionaire on paper, guaranteeing the country’s social infrastructure forever. Or look to the Gulf States, such as Qatar, where the native population is effectively subsidized by the land itself. Now, we must take these petrostate models and upgrade them for the AI techno-state reality. While oil is a meaningful part of the world economy, it is tiny in comparison to what we are talking about here. The entire global economy is many times larger. So take that concept and expand it out many times over in scale. Artificial intelligence in this future state is not a slice of the pie. AI is the oven, the bakery, and the wheat. It touches everything—healthcare, law, coding, art, logistics. If Alaska can cut a check based on the profits of pumping sludge out of the ground, imagine the dividend potential when the resource is the entirety of the global economy. And at the same time, prices will come down radically because of the reduced cost of production and delivery, increasing the spending power of every dollar. This is a virtuous cycle if managed correctly. Because beyond any moral argument for ownership, there is a cold, hard economic reality that demands this change: the necessity of the closed loop of how an economy runs. This is not a liberal political position or a call for communist control, but rather a macroeconomic reality being articulated by thought leaders across the political spectrum. But herein lies the rub. Today, the top 10 percent own 88 percent of the stock market. That is what has to change as we move into an economy of such abundance. For the engine to work, we must have everyone invested in the economy as a whole—not through charity or dependence, but through a model that looks like Alaska or Norway and their oil. The alternative is quite bleak: high unemployment, extensive human suffering, and overwhelming social unrest. And I can assure you, as an entrepreneur, no one wins in that game. It is worth noting that, as I write this, the current administration has created a program where a $1,000 investment in the S&P 500 per child born during a certain window will give these children a stake of ownership in American capitalism. And it has created a structure to allow billionaires to contribute as well; Michael Dell and his wife have committed $6.25 billion to give an even larger group of children an ownership stake. 102 This is the model to watch closely. In a world of AI abundance, the cost of goods drops close to the cost of raw materials and energy. A dividend check in 2035 might buy five times what the same amount buys today. But that deflation only works if there is money in motion. If AI produces everything but humans earn nothing, the cycle breaks. The dividend isn’t charity; it’s the spark plug that keeps the engine firing. Crucially, this does not mean we are aiming for a world of homogeneity or equality of outcome. The goal is not to make everyone the same; the goal is to give everyone a stake. And those who create will have a radically bigger stake as individuals, much like Bezos at Amazon. Once that dividend is paid—once the partial ownership is distributed—humanity will continue to express itself. Some will take that capital and reinvest it to build massive new wealth. Others will spend it all. Some will focus on the creative arts, others on growing gardens. Some will dedicate their lives to physical health and competitive sports, while others will focus on raising children and increasing time with loved ones. Humans will still get to live, strive, and make choices. But for the first time in history, exchanging work for income might not have to be one of them. We will have the opportunity to live higher up on Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. It is important to note that in this state of abundance, the national debt and its overwhelming debt service likely diminish dramatically. Today, we spend more on debt service than we spend on our military each year. Much of what the federal government spends would either go away or become much cheaper. We could replace that expense with equity purchasing programs distributed to the American people. Ownership. One of the great challenges, of course, is how we get from here to there. The path forward is obscured by the anxiety of the transition period—that dangerous gap where human jobs vanish before the new structures of ownership fully appear. Imagine a time when we have 15–20 percent unemployment from AI, but most people still work, and the massive deflationary cost-of-living reductions have not yet been realized. Our government will face a tremendous challenge: how to be fair to those who work while supporting those who don’t. I think we must begin to use our government to secure and distribute ownership incentives gradually, to those employed and unemployed, across all economic classes. This is not a handout, and it is not needs-based. It is a redirection of wasteful government spending toward distributed investment in the US economy for its citizens.
